content: Abnormal biliary secretion in individuals with cystic fibrosis leads to the thickening of bile and the formation of plugs within the bile ducts. This obstruction and the resulting abnormal bile flow contribute to the development of cystic fibrosis-related liver disease. This condition is most commonly observed during adolescence, with up to 20% of adolescents with cystic fibrosis developing chronic liver disease. If left untreated, early liver changes can progress to end-stage liver disease, necessitating liver transplantation. One therapeutic option currently in use is ursodeoxycholic acid. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether ursodeoxycholic acid improves liver function, reduces the risk of chronic liver disease, and enhances overall outcomes in individuals with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, electronic databases, handsearches of relevant journals, conference abstracts, and online trial registries. The most recent search of the trials register was performed on April 9, 2017. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared the use of ursodeoxycholic acid for at least three months with either a placebo or no additional treatment in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials, and the GRADE system was used to evaluate the quality of the evidence. A total of 12 trials were identified, but only four trials involving 137 participants met the inclusion criteria. Data were available from three of these trials, encompassing 118 participants, as one cross-over trial did not provide appropriate data for analysis. The dosage of ursodeoxycholic acid ranged from 10 to 20 mg/kg/day, administered for up to 12 months. However, the complex design of two trials limited the analysis to subsets of participants. The results showed no significant difference in weight change, with a mean difference of -0.90 kg (95% confidence interval: -1.94 to 0.14) based on data from 30 participants in two trials. Improvement in biliary excretion was reported in only one trial, but no significant changes were observed after treatment. Furthermore, no data were available for long-term outcomes, such as mortality or the need for liver transplantation. The authors concluded that there is a lack of sufficient trials assessing the effectiveness of ursodeoxycholic acid in this context. The quality of the available evidence ranged from low to very low. As a result, there is currently insufficient evidence to support the routine use of ursodeoxycholic acid in individuals with cystic fibrosis.
